findings.title: [P1] Reject non-finite timeout values instead of returning them
findings.body: Triggered by any input where `Number(value)` is not finite. `parseTimeout("abc")` now returns `NaN`; `parseTimeout("Infinity")` returns `Infinity`; `parseTimeout("1e309")` returns `Infinity`. Previously all of these threw `"invalid timeout"` under the unconditional `!Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) || timeout <= 0` guard (parseInt of a non-numeric string is `NaN`). Because `Number.isFinite(timeout)` guards the throw rather than participating in the rejection, validation is skipped precisely for invalid values — the function's documented-by-behavior contract "returns a positive safe integer or throws" is broken. The PR description explicitly claims to preserve existing contracts. Callers receive `NaN`/`±Infinity` and can no longer trust the return value; when such a value reaches Node timers it is coerced to a 1 ms delay (immediate-fire) rather than failing loudly.

findings.title: [P2] `Number(value)` changes the accepted parsing grammar vs `parseInt(value, 10)`
findings.body: Independent of the NaN/Infinity leak, the parser swap changes outcomes for finite inputs. Previously-accepted values now throw: `"1.5"` returned `1` (parseInt truncates) but now throws (finite, not an integer); `"5e-1"` similarly went `5` → throw. Previously-rejected values now return different numbers: `"1e3"` went `1` → `1000`; `"0x10"`/`"0b10"`/`"0o10"` threw under base-10 parseInt (`0` or `NaN` → reject) but now return `16`/`2`/`8`; `"12abc"` returned `12` but now returns `NaN`. (Plain integers, `undefined`, and empty/whitespace strings keep their prior outcomes — `""` still throws via `0 <= 0`.) Any existing configuration relying on the old grammar silently changes meaning or starts failing. If strict base-10 integer parsing is intended, keep `Number.parseInt(value, 10)`; if full-string numeric parsing is intended, the grammar change should be deliberate and documented.

findings.title: [P3] Add regression coverage for the changed parsing/validation contract
findings.body: The repository has no tests at all (`src/options.ts` is the only file), so nothing pins the behavior this PR changes. A small table-driven test over `undefined`, valid integers, `"1.5"`, `"1e3"`, `"0x10"`, `""`, `"abc"`, `"Infinity"`, and unsafe-large values would have caught the P1 immediately (every `"abc"`-style case expects a throw that no longer happens) and would lock down whichever grammar is chosen.
